title: Peer Pressure and Resisting It
keyIdea: Peer pressure is the push you feel from people your own age to think or act like them. It can help you, like friends getting you to try a new club, or harm you, like a dare to take something or share a mean photo. Harmful pushes use a few tricks: dares and teasing, "everyone does it", "just this once" and "real friends would". In a famous study, about 3 in 4 people went along with a group's clearly wrong answer at least once, but one person on their side made going along far rarer. You can resist with a calm no, a joke and a new plan, or by walking away, and you tell a trusted adult when someone could be hurt.
familyTip: Swap stories at dinner: each person tells a time a friend pushed them, once in a good way and once in a bad way, and what they did. Then practise three ways to say no to a dare, out loud, in a calm voice: a plain no, a joke with a new plan, and simply walking off. Agree a code word your child can text you if they need an easy way out of a situation.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort helpful from harmful pushes, name the trick, trust your eyes against a crowd, hold your line, decide where the line is.

kid: Peer pressure is the push you feel from people your age to act like them. Sometimes they say it out loud. Sometimes you just feel it, because you want to fit in.
Not all of it is bad. A friend who gets you to join a club or try the climbing wall is a helpful push. A harmful push gets you to do something unkind, risky or against the rules.

Harmful pushes use tricks. A dare calls you scared. Everyone does it makes you feel odd for saying no, and it is often not even true. Just this once makes it sound small. Real friends would uses your friendship as a prize. Once you can name the trick, it is easier to say no.

Groups are strong. In one study, people saw a group give a clearly wrong answer, and about 3 in 4 went along at least once. But with just one person on their side, most stuck with the truth. So be that one person for a friend. To say no, keep it calm and short, use a joke and a new plan, or walk away. If someone could get hurt, tell a trusted adult.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. The PSHE Association programme for Key Stage 2 asks pupils to spot and manage dares and pressure from friends. They should also know ways to respond, and when and how to ask for help. Key terms: peer pressure, dare, social norm, assertive, trusted adult.

Pressure from peers can be spoken, like a dare, or unspoken, like the wish to fit in. It can be good as well as bad. Social norms research by Perkins and Berkowitz found that young people often think more of their peers take risks than really do. That is why 'everyone does it' works so well. In Asch's line studies in the 1950s, people went along with a wrong group on about a third of key trials. About 3 in 4 went along at least once. With one honest partner, that fell to about 1 in 20.

Common mistakes: thinking all peer pressure is bad, so children miss the good kind and cannot tell the two apart; thinking that saying no means a big fight, when insults tend to make the push stronger; accepting 'just once' as if it does not count; staying quiet when a friend is pushed, though one ally is the best defence; and keeping a secret when someone is being hurt. Be careful not to treat giving in as a flaw. Adults go along with groups too. The skill is to spot the trick and have a plan.

In the lab your child sorts six pushes as helpful or harmful and names the trick in four messages. Then they judge line lengths while five classmates give a wrong answer, and again with one ally. They pick replies to three rising pushes, and decide if eight choices are fine to copy or need a no or a trusted adult. Each wrong choice gets a reason that names the slip.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a helpful push from friends?
choices: Getting you to join the choir with them
Daring you to climb the school fence
Telling you to leave a new kid out
practice.hint: Which one leads to something good for you and harms nobody?
practice.explain: Joining the choir is good for you and hurts nobody. That is positive peer pressure.

practice.prompt: This week Leo felt {n} pushes from friends. {k} were harmful and he said no to each. How many pushes were helpful?
practice.hint: Every push was either helpful or harmful. Take away the harmful ones.
practice.explain: {n} pushes take away {k} harmful ones leaves {=n-k} helpful pushes.

practice.prompt: "Go on, are you scared?" Which trick is this?
choices: A dare or tease
"Just this once"
A helpful push
practice.hint: It calls you a name so you feel you must prove it wrong.
practice.explain: Calling you scared is a dare or tease. It makes saying no feel like losing.

practice.prompt: A group of {n} friends tries to get you to skip class. One of them, Asha, says no with you. How many are still pushing?
practice.hint: Asha is now on your side. Take her away from the group.
practice.explain: {n} friends minus Asha leaves {=n-1} still pushing, and now you have an ally.

practice.prompt: Which reply to a dare is calm and firm?
choices: "No thanks. I'm going to play football."
"Fine, but only once."
"You're all so stupid."
practice.hint: Look for a clear no that does not insult anyone.
practice.explain: A short no with a new plan is calm and firm. Giving in or insulting makes it worse.

choices: A push from people your age to act like them
A rule set by your teacher
Your own idea to try something
pool.hint: Peers are people your own age.
pool.explain: Peer pressure comes from people your own age, and can be helpful or harmful.

pool.prompt: "Everyone in our year has done it." Why is this a trick?
choices: It is often not true, and it is still your choice
It is always true
It means it must be safe
pool.hint: Do people often guess more of their friends do risky things than really do?
pool.explain: People often overestimate how many peers do risky things, and even if many did, you still decide.

pool.prompt: In the line study, what helped people most to give their own answer?
choices: One other person agreeing with them
Being in a bigger group
Waiting to answer last
pool.hint: Think about the round where one person said B.
pool.explain: With one ally, going along with the wrong group fell from about 1 in 3 answers to about 1 in 20.

pool.prompt: A friend tells you someone is hurting them and says, "Don't tell anyone." What should you do?
choices: Tell a trusted adult
Keep the secret
Post about it online
pool.hint: Is this a secret that keeps someone safe, or one that keeps them in danger?
pool.explain: When someone is being hurt, tell a trusted adult. That is not breaking a friendship.

pool.prompt: You practise {n} ways to say no, and use {k} of them in a role-play. How many have you still to try?
pool.hint: Take the ones you used away from the ones you practised.
pool.explain: {n} ways take away {k} used leaves {=n-k} still to try.

pool.prompt: "If you were my real friend, you would." Which reply works best?
choices: "I am your friend. I'm still not doing it."
"OK, I'll prove it."
"Then I hate you."
pool.hint: You can keep the friendship and the no at the same time.
pool.explain: A real friend accepts your no. You can say you are friends and still refuse.

pool.prompt: {n} kids are teased into a dare. Each one has a friend who says no with them, making pairs. How many people are saying no?
pool.hint: Each kid plus their ally makes two people.
pool.explain: {n} pairs of 2 make {=2*n} people saying no together.

pool.prompt: Your friends all wear the same trainers, so you want some too. Is this OK?
choices: Usually fine: nobody is hurt and you still choose
Never OK: all peer influence is bad
Only OK if you lie about the price
pool.hint: Ask: could someone be hurt? Would I feel bad later?
pool.explain: Copying friends in harmless ways is normal. The line is when someone could be hurt.

pool.prompt: Why does walking away count as resisting?
choices: You leave the pressure and keep your choice
It shows you agree
It means you lost
pool.hint: Do you have to win an argument to say no?
pool.explain: Walking away ends the push without a fight, and you still did not give in.
